p.seg: The Parable of the Fool Eating Salt
Once there was a foolish man
who came to another's house.
The host served him food,
but he found it bland and tasteless.
When the host heard this,
he added more salt.
Once the man tasted the salt and found the food delicious,
he thought to himself:
“The reason it is tasty
is because there is salt.
If a little is so good,
how much better must it be with more?”
Lacking wisdom,
the fool then ate salt by itself,
and after eating, his mouth became parched
and it caused him harm instead.
This is like those outsiders
who hear that moderation in food and drink leads to the Path,
and who then immediately stop eating,
sometimes for seven days,
sometimes for fifteen days,
bringing only hunger and suffering upon themselves
with no benefit to the Path.
Just as that fool,
who, believing the taste to come from salt, ate it alone
and thereby made his mouth parched,
so it is also with them.
Once there was a foolish man
who planned to receive guests.
He wished to collect cow’s milk
to offer at the gathering.
He had this thought:
“If now I milk the cow a little each day in advance,
the milk will gradually increase,
but at last I will have nowhere to store it,
and it might even sour and spoil.
Better to let the cow accumulate the milk in her belly,
and when the time comes,
I can draw it all at once.”
With this thought,
he took the cow and her calf
and tied them in separate places.
After a month,
he set up the gathering
and invited his guests.
Then he led the cow over
to draw the milk,
but the cow’s udder was completely dry.
The assembled guests either grew angry or laughed at him.
So it is with the fool
who wishes to practice charity
and says,
“Let me wait until I have great wealth,
then I shall donate it all at once.”
Before he has accrued much,
perhaps the authorities, disaster, or thieves steal it away,
or suddenly he meets his end
and has no chance to make his gift.
This is the same.
Once there was a foolish man
who had no hair on his head.
Once, someone
hit him on the head with a pear.
This happened two, three times,
leaving his head wounded and broken.
Yet the fool silently endured,
not thinking to dodge or leave.
A bystander saw this,
and said to him:
“Why not avoid it?
You just stand there and get hit,
letting your head get broken.”
The fool replied:
“That person is arrogant and relies on his strength,
ignorant and lacking wisdom.
Because he sees that I have no hair on my head,
he thinks it is a stone,
and so strikes with the pear and breaks my head.”
The bystander said:
“You are the fool yourself.
How can you call him the fool?
If you were not foolish,
being struck by another,
to the point your head is broken,
would you not know to flee or dodge?”
So it is with the bhikṣu,
who does not fully cultivate morality, learning, and wisdom,
but merely sets his deportment in order
to attract gain and profit.
Like that foolish man
who, when struck on the head,
does not know to escape,
until he is wounded and broken,
yet calls the other the fool—
this bhikṣu is also thus.
Once there was a foolish man
whose wife was beautiful,
and he loved her dearly.
The wife, however, lacked chastity and fidelity,
and later, while at home, consorted with another man.
Her desire for illicit affairs was great,
and she wished to follow her lover
and leave her own husband.
She secretly confided in an old woman, saying:
“After I am gone,
please bring a dead woman’s corpse and put it in the house,
then tell my husband
that I have died.”
The old woman, watching for a time when the husband was away,
placed a corpse
in the home.
When the husband returned,
the old woman told him:
“Your wife is dead.”
The husband then went to look,
believed it was his wife,
and mourned bitterly,
gathering wood and oil
to burn the remains,
gathered the bones into a bag,
and carried them close day and night.
When the wife later grew weary of her lover,
she returned home,
and said to her husband:
“I am your wife.”
He replied:
“My wife has long been dead;
who are you
to falsely claim to be my wife?”
Even after she insisted several times,
he still did not believe her.
This is like those outsiders
who, hearing false teachings
become confused in their hearts,
mistake them for truth
and will not change forever.
Even upon hearing correct doctrine,
they do not believe or accept it.
In the past, there was someone
who, lacking wisdom,
was extremely thirsty for water.
Seeing a mirage in the heat,
he thought it was water,
and chased after it,
until he reached the Xīn Tóu River.
When he arrived at the river,
he just looked at it and did not drink.
A bystander said:
“You suffered thirst and chased water,
now you have reached water,
why do you not drink?”
The fool answered:
“Please, you drink it all,
then I will drink.
There is so much water,
it cannot be drunk all at once,
so I do not drink.”
Those around, hearing his words, all laughed heartily at him.
This is like those outsiders who distort the principles,
since they themselves cannot uphold the Buddha’s precepts,
so refuse to accept them,
causing themselves in future to lack the portion of attainment,
and so circle in birth and death.
Like that fool
who, seeing water but not drinking
and laughed at for it,
so it is with them.
Once there was a foolish man
who was raising seven sons.
One son died first.
When this fool saw his son had died,
he wished to keep the body at home,
and leave himself.
A bystander saw this
and said to him:
“The paths of life and death are different.
You ought quickly to arrange
to carry him far away
and bury him,
so how can you keep the body
and leave yourself?”
When the foolish man heard this,
he thought to himself:
“If I cannot keep him
and must bury him,
then I must kill one more son
so that I can balance the load on both ends
and manage to carry them.”
And so he killed another son,
carried them,
and buried them far away in the wilds.
Onlookers saw this
and laughed at him deeply,
for such a thing was unheard of.
For example, suppose a bǐqiū
secretly violates a precept,
hesitates to repent,
and silently conceals the offense
while claiming himself to be pure.
If someone knows of it,
he immediately admonishes, saying:
"A renunciant should guard and uphold the precepts
as one would protect a bright jewel,
not allowing it to be chipped or lost.
Why do you now violate the precepts you received and refuse to repent?"
The offender replies:
"If I must confess,
I will violate it again
and then declare it."
Thus he proceeds to break the precepts
and commits much wrongdoing,
and only then confesses it.
This is like a foolish man:
when one son dies,
he kills another son.
This bǐqiū is exactly the same.
In the past, there was a man
of fine appearance
and perfect wisdom,
who also possessed great wealth,
so that everyone who heard of him praised him without exception.
At that time, a foolish man
saw him thus
and called him his brother.
The reason being:
since the man had wealth,
he could use it when needed,
so he called him brother; but when he saw him repay debts, he claimed he was not his brother.
A bystander said:
"You are a fool!
How can you call another your brother just for his wealth?
And when it comes time to repay debts,
you then deny he is your brother."
The fool replied:
"I desired to obtain his wealth and so claimed him as my brother,
but in truth he is not.
When it comes time for debts,
then I say he is not my brother."
All who heard this
laughed at it.
It is just like the wàidào:
who, upon hearing the good words of the Fó,
greedily steal and use them
as if their own,
and when others beside them urge them to practice,
they refuse to practice,
but say:
"For the sake of profit and support,
I take the Buddha's words
to teach and guide living beings,
yet with no real substance,
so why should I practice?"
Just as the previous fool,
for the sake of gaining wealth,
called the man brother,
but when it came to repaying debts,
again denied he was brother,
so it is here.
In a past age, there was a mountain qiāng,
who stole from the royal treasury
and fled far away.
Then, the king sent men in all directions to track and catch him,
and brought him before the king.
The king then pressed him on where he got the clothes he wore,
and the mountain qiāng replied:
"These clothes are from my ancestors."
The king had him put them on,
but since they were not originally his,
he did not know how to wear them:
what should have gone on his hands he put on his feet,
what should have been at his waist he put upon his head.
The king, seeing this thief,
gathered his ministers
and deliberated over this matter,
saying:
"If these clothes have truly belonged to your ancestors,
you should know how to put them on.
Why do you wear them upside-down,
using the upper as the lower?
Because you do not understand,
it is clear these clothes are stolen,
and not your original property."
As an analogy:
the king is like the Fó,
the treasury like the Dharma,
and the foolish qiāng just like the wàidào,
who secretly listen to the Buddha's Dharma
and incorporate it into their own teachings
claiming it as their own,
but because they do not understand,
when they arrange the Buddha's Dharma,
they confuse top and bottom,
not knowing the true nature of Dharma.
Just as the mountain qiāng,
having obtained the king's precious garments,
did not know their order
and wore them upside-down,
so it is here as well.
In ancient times,
there was a man among the people
who praised his father's virtue,
saying:
"My father was compassionate and kind,
did not harm or steal,
spoke honestly and truthfully,
and practiced generosity."
Then a foolish man,
hearing this,
thought to himself:
"My father's virtue and conduct surpass even yours."
People asked:
"What virtue does he have?
Please tell us."
The fool replied:
"From childhood, my father cut off all desire for lust
and was never defiled."
The people said:
"If he severed lust,
how were you born?"
Everyone at the time was deeply astonished and laughed.
Just like those in the world lacking wisdom,
who seek to praise others' virtues
without truly understanding,
but only bring about criticism;
like that fool,
who wished to praise his father,
yet his words became fault,
so it is here.
In times past, there was a foolish rich man
ignorant of all things,
who came to another wealthy household
and saw a three-story building,
tall, broad, adorned and beautiful,
spacious and open,
and his heart yearned for it.
He thought to himself:
"I have wealth and money
not less than theirs,
so why have I not built such a building?"
He called a carpenter
and asked:
"Can you build a fine house like that one?"
The carpenter replied:
"That is my work."
He immediately said,
"Build a house for me like that one."
So the carpenter began by leveling the ground and making bricks for the building.
The fool saw the making of bricks for the house,
but still doubted in his heart
and could not understand,
so he asked:
"What are you making?"
The carpenter replied:
"A three-story house."
The fool said again:
"I do not want the lower two stories—
first make the top floor for me."
The carpenter replied:
"That is not possible—
how can you get a second floor without making the first?
Without making the second,
how can you get the third?"
But the fool insisted,
"I do not want the lower two, you must make only the top for me."
On hearing this,
everyone burst into laughter,
all saying:
"How can there be an upper floor without building the first below?"
Just as the fourfold disciples of the Shìzūn,
who do not diligently honor the Three Jewels,
are lazy and negligent,
yet seek the fruits of the Path,
and say,
"I do not want the lower three fruits,
I only seek the fruit of Āluóhàn."
They too are laughed at by the people of the time,
being no different than such fools.
In the past, there was a bōluómén
who claimed to know much,
and was thoroughly proficient in the various arts and astrology,
and, relying on himself as such,
sought to display his virtue.
He traveled to another country,
carrying his child and weeping.
Someone asked the bōluómén,
"Why are you crying?"
The Póluómén said:
"This child will die in seven days.
Out of pity for his premature death,
I cry only for this reason."
The people at the time said:
"Human lifespan is hard to know,
calculations are often mistaken.
Even if seven days pass, perhaps he will not die.
Why cry in advance?"
Póluómén said:
"The sun and moon may be darkened,
the stars may fall,
yet what I have calculated will never go awry."
For the sake of fame and profit,
at the end of seven days,
he killed his own child
to validate his own words.
Then all the people of the world, after seven days, heard the child had died,
and they all sighed and said:
"Truly he is a wise man;
what he said was not wrong."
Their hearts gave rise to faith and obedience,
and they all came to pay respect.
Just like the fourfold disciples of Fótuó,
for the sake of gains and offerings,
falsely claim attainment of the Way;
having the dharma of fools,
they kill good men,
falsely displaying benevolence and virtue,
causing in future endless suffering,
like Póluómén, who killed his son to validate his words and delude the world.
In ancient times, there was a fool
boiling black stone honey.
There was a wealthy man
who came to his house.
The fool then thought:
"Now I shall take black stone honey syrup and give it to this rich man."
So he added a little water
and placed it on the fire.
Then, above the fire, he fanned it
hoping to cool it.
A bystander said:
"If you do not remove the fire below
but keep on fanning above,
how can it possibly cool?"
Everyone laughed at him.
This is just like the non-Buddhists who do not extinguish the raging fire of afflictions;
they perform a little ascetic practice,
lying on thorns,
burning themselves with five fires,
hoping for the cool and tranquil Path.
But this is impossible;
they are only ridiculed by the wise,
suffering now,
with calamity flowing into future ages.
In the past there was a man,
who sat in a house together with a large group of people.
They praised an outsider’s virtue and conduct, which were extremely good,
saying, "He only has two faults:
first, he is prone to anger;
second, he acts hastily."
At that time, this man happened to be outside the door,
and hearing these words,
he gave rise to anger,
entered the house at once,
seized the one who spoke ill of him,
and struck him with his hands.
An onlooker asked:
"Why are you hitting him?"
The man replied:
"When have I ever been prone to anger or acted hastily?
Yet this person claims, 'I am prone to anger and act hastily.'
That is why I hit him."
Bystanders said:
"Right now you have clearly displayed the signs of anger and hastiness;
how can you deny it?"
When one reacts to having their faults pointed out with resentment and blame,
it brings deep bewilderment and ridicule from everyone.
Just like a man in the world who drinks alcohol,
addicted and enthralled by wine,
committing every sort of lax behavior,
and when people admonish him,
he instead becomes angry and resentful,
struggling to justify himself,
trying to make himself appear blameless.
Such a fool
denies hearing his own faults;
when he sees others pointing them out,
he wants to strike them in return.
In the past, there was a merchant
who wished to enter the great sea.
The method for entering the great sea requires a guide,
and only then can one go.
So they together sought and found a guide.
When they found him,
they led him along
and set out to the wilderness.
There they encountered a celestial shrine
that required a human sacrifice for passage.
The merchants then deliberated:
"We are all close companions;
how can we kill one of our own?
Only the guide should be used to sacrifice to the heavens."
So they killed the guide
and used him for worship.
When the ritual was done,
they lost their way
and did not know where to go.
Worn out and desperate, they all died.
All people in the world are the same:
wishing to enter the Dharma sea to obtain its precious treasures,
one must cultivate wholesome dharma and good conduct as a guide.
If one destroys good conduct,
one will endlessly wander in the wilderness of birth and death with no hope of escape,
passing through the three evil destinies,
enduring long suffering,
just like those merchants,
about to enter the great sea,
who killed their guide,
lost their path,
and finally died of distress.
In former times, there was a king
who had a daughter.
He called the physician and said:
"Give me medicine
to make her quickly grow up."
The physician replied:
"I have a good medicine that can make her immediately mature,
but at the moment I do not have it,
I need to seek and search for it.
While I go to get the medicine,
the king must not look at her.
Wait until I have given her the medicine
and only then show her to the king."
Thereupon he went to a distant place to get the medicine,
and after twelve years,
he got the medicine and returned
and gave it to the girl to take.
Then he presented her to the king;
the king, seeing her, was joyful
and said to himself:
"He truly is a good physician;
he gave my daughter medicine
and made her quickly grow up."
So he ordered his attendants to give him treasures and jewels.
All the people of the time laughed at the king's lack of wisdom,
not knowing how to reckon the years from birth,
and, seeing her grown,
thought it was the power of the medicine.
People in the world are the same:
they go to a spiritual teacher
and ask,
"I wish to seek the Way;
please instruct and guide me,
so that I may attain it immediately."
The good spiritual teacher, using skillful means, teaches them to sit in meditation and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination,
gradually accumulating virtue,
and attaining Arhatship.
Overjoyed,
they say:
"Excellent, Master!
You have swiftly enabled me to realize the most wondrous Dharma."
In former times there were two men
who together planted sugarcane,
and made an agreement:
"Whoever plants well will be rewarded;
whoever does not,
shall be heavily punished."
Among the two, one thought:
"Sugarcane is extremely sweet;
if I press out its juice
and pour it back onto the sugarcane plants,
the taste will surely be much enhanced,
and I will surpass the other."
So he pressed the sugarcane,
took the juice and used it for watering,
hoping for richer flavor,
but instead, he ruined the roots,
and all the sugarcane was lost.
People in the world are the same:
wishing to seek good fortune and blessings,
relying on their own wealth and power,
they exercise coercion and force,
oppressing the common people,
seizing their wealth and property,
using it for making merit,
hoping for good results.
But they do not know that, in the future, they will instead receive disaster and harm,
just like pressing the sugarcane,
which ruins both sides.
In the past, there was a merchant
to whom someone owed half a coin.
After a long time, it could not be repaid.
He then went to collect the debt.
Ahead was a great river;
he hired help for two coins
and was then able to cross.
When he arrived to collect the debt,
he never got to see the debtor,
so he came back and crossed the river again,
once more hiring help for two coins.
For a debt of half a coin, he lost four coins;
along with the fatigue and exhaustion of the journey,
what was owed was very little,
but what was lost was exceedingly much.
As a result, he was mocked and ridiculed by everyone.
Worldly people are also like this:
for the sake of small fame or profit,
they bring ruin to great undertakings;
they think only of themselves,
without regard for propriety and righteousness,
so they receive a bad reputation in the present
and bitter retribution in the end.
In the past, there was a man
who was poor and destitute,
serving Wáng as a laborer.
After many days and months,
his body became emaciated.
Wáng saw this and pitied him,
so granted him a dead camel.
Once the poor man received it,
he immediately began to skin it,
but, disliking that his knife was dull,
he sought a whetstone to sharpen it.
So he obtained a whetstone atop a tower,
sharpened his knife until it was sharp,
and went down to continue skinning.
Thus, he repeatedly went back and forth to sharpen his knife;
after a while, he grew even more fatigued and weary,
and became unable to keep climbing up.
He then hoisted the camel up to the tower,
so that he could sharpen his knife on the stone right there,
and was deeply ridiculed and laughed at by everyone.
Just like the foolish person
who breaks precepts and moral restraints,
acquiring much wealth,
and then uses it to cultivate merit
in hopes of being born in the heavens:
it is like hoisting a camel up to the tower to sharpen the knife:
much effort is expended,
yet what is gained is very little.
In the past, someone sailed a boat across the sea,
and lost a silver armlet,
which dropped into the water.
He then reflected:
"Now I will mark the water as a sign,
leave it for now,
and later I shall retrieve it."
After two months of travel,
he arrived in the countries of the Shīzǐ.
He saw a river,
went into the river,
and searched for the armlet he had lost before.
The people all asked him:
"What are you searching for?"
He replied:
"I lost my armlet earlier,
now I wish to retrieve it."
They asked:
"Where did you lose it?"
He answered:
"I lost it when I first entered the sea."
Then they asked again:
"How long ago did you lose it?"
He said:
"It has been two months since I lost it."
They asked:
"Since it's been two months since you lost it,
how can you find it here?"
He replied:
"When I lost my armlet,
I marked the water as a sign,
and the water here is no different than what I marked before,
so I am searching here."
They further asked:
"Although the water is not different,
when you lost it before,
it was over there,
but now you are searching here
—how can you possibly find it?"
Then all the people burst into loud laughter.
Likewise, heretics
who do not practice the true path,
and amidst things that only appear good, recklessly inflict hardship upon themselves,
seeking liberation;
it is just like that foolish person
who lost his armlet there,
but searches for it here.
In the past, there was a man
who spoke of the crimes of Wáng,
saying this:
"Wáng is extremely cruel and brutal,
his governance without justice."
When Wáng heard this,
he became very enraged,
but never investigated who had spoken these words.
Instead, he listened to slanderous flatterers,
and seized a worthy minister,
commanding that his back be flayed
and a hundred taels of flesh be taken.
Someone testified that these words had not been spoken,
and Wáng immediately regretted it,
and demanded a thousand taels of flesh
to patch up the minister's back.
At night, the man groaned loudly
in great torment and pain.
Wáng heard his cries,
and asked:
"Why do you suffer so much?
I took a hundred taels from you,
and now give you ten times that,
yet you are still not content?
Why do you suffer so?"
A bystander replied:
"Great Wáng!
If you cut off a son's head,
even if given a thousand new heads,
you cannot avoid the son's death.
Though you give ten times the flesh,
the pain cannot be prevented."
Foolish people are just the same:
not fearing a future life,
greedy only for present pleasures,
causing suffering to all beings,
overburdening the people,
and amassing wealth and goods,
hoping thereby to extinguish their crimes
and obtain good fortune in return.
It is just like that Wáng
who cut another's back
and took his flesh,
then used more flesh to patch it,
hoping to make it painless—
such a thing is impossible.
Long ago, in an earlier age, there was a woman
who had just one child,
but wished for more children.
She asked the other women:
"Who is able to grant me another child?"
An old woman said to her:
"I can make it so you will surely have another child;
you must offer sacrifice to Heaven."
She asked the old woman:
"What must I use for the sacrifice?"
The old woman replied:
"Kill your son
and use his blood to offer to Heaven,
and you will certainly have many more children."
Then this woman prepared to follow that advice and wanted to kill her son.
Someone wise nearby
ridiculed and scolded her:
"Foolish and ignorant,
how did you come to such ends?
Can you possibly obtain unborn children
by killing the one you have now?"
The fool is just the same:
for the sake of pleasures not yet born, he throws himself into a pit of fire,
doing all kinds of harm to himself
just to be reborn in heaven.
"Bǎiyù Jīng," Scroll One, Preface. Thus I have heard:
Once, the Buddha was staying at Wángshèchéng,
in the Magpie Sealed Bamboo Grove, together with great bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the eight kinds of beings, thirty-six thousand in all.
At that time, in the assembly were five hundred heterodox Brāhmaṇas,
who rose from their seats
and addressed the Buddha:
"We have heard the Buddha's Way is vast and profound,
unmatched by any.
Thus we have come to seek and inquire,
and hope only that you will explain it to us."
The Buddha said: "Very good."
They asked: "Is the world existent or nonexistent?"
The Buddha answered:
"It is both existent and nonexistent."
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"If it is as it is now—existent—how can you say it is nonexistent? If it is as it is now—nonexistent—how can you say it is existent?"
The Buddha answered:
"For the living, it is said to exist;
for the dead, it is said to not exist;
thus it is said
sometimes existent, sometimes nonexistent."
They asked:
"From what are people born?"
The Buddha replied:
"People are born from grains."
They asked:
"From what are the five grains born?"
The Buddha replied:
"The five grains are born from the four elements—fire and wind."
Question:
“From where do the four great elements—fire and wind—arise?”
Answer:
“The four great elements—fire and wind—arise from emptiness.”
Question:
“From where does emptiness arise?”
Answer:
“It arises from non-possession.”
Question:
“From where does non-possession arise?”
Answer:
“It arises from zìrán.”
Question:
“From where does zìrán arise?”
Answer:
“It arises from Níyuán.”
Question:
“From where does Níyuán arise?”
The Buddha said:
“Why do you now question
to such a profound extent?
Níyuán is the dharma of neither birth nor death.”
Question:
“Has the Buddha attained Níyuán yet?”
Answer:
“I have not yet attained Níyuán.”
“If you have not yet attained Níyuán,
how do you know Níyuán is constant and blissful?”
The Buddha said:
“Now I ask you:
Are all beings in the world suffering or joyful?”
Answer:
“Beings greatly suffer.”
The Buddha said:
“How do you define suffering?”
Answer:
“I have seen that when beings die, the pain is unbearable;
therefore I know death is suffering.”
The Buddha said:
“Though you have not died,
yet you know the suffering of death;
I have seen the Buddhas of the ten directions who neither arise nor perish,
thus I know that Níyuán is always blissful.”
The five hundred Brāhmaṇas’ hearts opened and understanding dawned;
they sought to receive the five precepts,
awakened to srotaāpanna fruit,
and resumed sitting as before.
The Buddha said:
“All of you, listen well!
Now I will extensively explain for you with various parables.”

Once there was the son of a wealthy elder,
who entered the sea to obtain scented wood.
After amassing it for years,
he finally acquired a cartload,
and brought it home.
He went to the market to sell it,
but because it was precious,
there was suddenly no buyer.
Many days passed without making a sale.
His heart grew weary and dejected,
and he became troubled.
He saw that those selling charcoal made quick sales,
so he thought to himself:
“It would be better to burn it for charcoal;
that way it could be sold quickly.”
So he burned it into charcoal.
Going to the market to sell it,
it did not fetch even half the price of a cartload of charcoal.
Foolish people in the world are just like this:
Through countless skillful means, they practice diligently
and aspire to the Buddha fruit.
But as it is difficult to attain,
they become discouraged,
thinking, “It would be better to strive for the śrāvaka fruit, swiftly cut off birth and death, and become an āluóhàn.”
Once there was a thief
who entered a wealthy household
and stole brocade.
He immediately used it to wrap old, tattered woolen goods and treasures of various sorts,
and was laughed at by the wise.
Foolish people in the world are just like this:
They develop faith
and enter the Buddha’s teaching,
cultivating good dharmas and various merits;
but out of greed for gain,
they break the pure precepts and destroy those merits,
and are mocked by the world
just the same.
Once there was a fool,
who ate raw sesame seeds
and found them unpalatable;
he roasted them and found them tasty,
so he thought:
“It would be better to roast them before planting,
so that later I can obtain delicious seeds.”
He roasted and then planted them,
which could never sprout again.
So too with people in the world:
They see that the bodhisattva’s practice over countless kalpas
involves difficult and arduous effort,
and think it is not joyful;
then they think:
“Better to become an āluóhàn,
swiftly ending birth and death,
as this achievement is much easier.”
But afterward, wishing to seek the Buddha’s fruit,
in the end they cannot attain it,
like those burnt seeds
that can never sprout again;
thus are foolish people in the world.
Once there was a man
who needed fire, as well as cold water for something.
He preserved the fire overnight
and filled a jar with water for bathing
and set it on the fire.
Later, wishing to get fire,
he found the fire had extinguished;
wishing for cold water,
he saw the water was now hot.
He lost both fire and cold water.
People in the world are likewise:
Entering the Buddha’s teachings,
they leave home to seek the path;
having achieved renunciation,
they turn their thoughts back to wives, children, relatives, and worldly affairs and the pleasures of the five desires.
Thus, they lose the fire of merit and the water of precept-keeping;
those who are distracted by desire are just the same.
Once there was a man,
who wished to win the king’s favor.
He asked another:
“How may I gain this?”
Someone replied:
“If you want the king’s favor,
you should imitate the king’s manner.”
So, he later went before the king,
and saw the king’s eye twitching and so imitated it.
The king asked:
“Are you ill?
Do you have a disease?
Why is your eye twitching?”
He replied to the king:
“I do not have an illness,
nor am I diseased,
but wished to gain your favor,
and seeing your eye twitch,
thus I imitated you.”
The king, upon hearing this,
became greatly angered
and had him harmed in various ways
and banished him from the country.
People also are like this:
Wishing to be close to the Dharma King, the Buddha,
they seek his good dharma
to increase themselves,
and once close,
yet not understanding that the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, for sentient beings’ sake,
demonstrates all kinds of expedient means and reveals their faults,
perhaps hearing his teachings
and finding some words or sentences irregular,
immediately give rise to slander,
imitating such mistaken ways.
Because of this,
within the Buddha’s Dharma they forever lose the good,
and fall into the three evil destinies;
just as with imitating the king, so it is.
In ancient times there was a man
who was whipped by Wáng,
and after being whipped,
he covered the wound with horse dung
wishing for a quick recovery.
There was a foolish man who saw this
and felt delighted in his heart,
and immediately said:
“I have certainly obtained the method for curing wounds.”
He then returned home
and said to his son:
“You whip my back;
I have found a good method
and now wish to try it.”
The son whipped his back,
and he covered it with horse dung,
thinking this was skillful.
People of the world are also like this:
upon hearing others say
to practice impurity contemplation,
and that it can immediately remove the wounds of the five aggregates' body,
they immediately say:
“I want to contemplate female beauty and the five desires.”
But before they see the impurity,
they are instead deluded and disturbed by women's beauty,
being swept along in birth and death,
falling into hells.
Foolish people in the world are likewise.
In the past there was a man,
whose wife was dignified in appearance
but had only an ugly nose.
When he went out,
he saw another woman who had a dignified appearance
and a very fine nose.
Then he thought to himself:
“Now would it not be good if I could cut off her nose
and put it on my wife's face,
would that not be excellent?”
So he cut off the other woman's nose,
brought it home,
and hurriedly called his wife:
“Quickly come out,
I’ll give you a fine nose.”
His wife came out,
and he immediately cut off her nose as well,
then tried to put the other nose on her face,
but it would not attach,
and so she lost her own nose too,
causing his wife great suffering and pain.
People in the world who are foolish are also like this:
hearing that some Śramaṇa or Brāhmaṇa of past times has great renown and virtue,
and is respected by everyone
receiving great gain and support,
then think to themselves:
“Now, I am no different from him.”
They falsely claim for themselves,
boastfully saying they have virtue,
but once they lose those benefits,
their conduct is also harmed.
Like cutting off another’s nose,
they only injure themselves in vain.
So too with foolish people in the world.
Long ago there was a man,
poor and destitute,
who worked for others as a servant,
and obtained a coarse hempen garment
which he wore.
Someone saw this
and said to him:
“You are of fine family
and of noble birth,
so why do you wear such a coarse, wretched robe?
Now I will teach you,
and ensure you obtain splendid clothes.
Follow my words,
I will never deceive you.”
The poor man was delighted
and respectfully obeyed his words.
The man then built a fire in front of him,
and said to the poor man:
“Now take off this coarse robe
and throw it into the fire.
In the burned place, you will get the most excellent garments.”
The poor man then took it off and threw it in the fire.
When it was burned,
he searched in the ashes for fine clothing,
but nothing was found at all.
People in the world are also thus:
from previous lives cultivating good deeds
they obtained this human body,
and should protect and advance virtue and their practice,
yet are deceived by outside paths, evil ones, and seductive women, who say:
“You must trust my words
and practice asceticism,
cast yourself from cliffs or into fire,
give up this life,
and you will be born in Brahma Heaven,
enjoying happiness forever.”
Believing these words,
they immediately forfeit their lives,
and after death
fall into hell,
suffering all kinds of torment.
Having lost the human body,
they gain nothing at all,
just like that poor man,
and likewise.
Long ago there was a man,
skilled at herding sheep,
and his sheep were many,
amounting to ten thousand.
He was extremely stingy and greedy,
unwilling to use anything for others.
At that time, there was a man
skilled in deceit and cunning.
He devised a scheme
and approached as a friend,
saying to him:
“Now, I am truly close and dear to you,
as if we are one body,
and there is no difference.
I know that in a certain household, there is a beautiful woman,
and I will seek her for you,
so you can have her as your wife.”
The shepherd
was pleased to hear this,
and generously gave sheep and other wealth.
That man then said again:
“Today your wife has given birth to a child.”
Although the shepherd had not seen his wife,
upon hearing the child had been born,
he was overjoyed
and gave that man more goods.
Later, the man said to him again:
“Your child, having been born, has now died.”
When the shepherd heard this,
he loudly wept and sobbed unceasingly.
People in the world are also like this:
though they diligently study and learn,
they hoard their teachings for fame and gain,
unwilling to teach and explain to others,
and are deluded by the leaks of their body
and vainly pursue worldly pleasure.
Like those who are deceived by their wife and child,
they lose good dharma,
and later lose both life and wealth,
thus lamenting bitterly
and experiencing sorrow and suffering,
just like the shepherd.
Once, there was a Brāhmaṇa teacher
who wished to hold a great assembly;
he said to his disciple:
“I need clay vessels for the assembly’s use.
You may hire a potter and go to the market to seek them.”
Then the disciple went to the potter’s house.
At that time there was a certain man,
whose donkey carried clay vessels
to the market intending to sell them,
but in a short while the donkey broke them all,
and he returned home
weeping and lamenting.
The disciple saw this
and asked him:
“Why do you lament and grieve so?”
The man replied:
“Through skillful effort, after many years of toil, I finally managed to make these pots,
and was taking them to market to sell.
But this wretched donkey, in a brief moment, broke all my pots,
and that is why I mourn.”
Then, when the disciple saw and heard this,
he rejoiced and said:
“This donkey is a fine creature:
what took so long to make, in a moment it can break.
I should buy this donkey now.”
The potter was pleased
and sold it to him.
He brought it home riding it,
and the teacher asked him:
“Why did you not bring the potter here?
What use is the donkey?”
The disciple replied:
“This donkey surpasses the potter:
what the potter takes so long to make, it can smash in a moment.”
The teacher said:
“You are utterly foolish and without wisdom!
This donkey now can break things,
but even given a hundred years, it cannot make a single one.”
Foolish people in this world are also thus:
even if, for hundreds of years, they are supported by others,
they never give anything in return,
always causing harm
and never bringing benefit,
just like those who repay kindness with betrayal.
In the past, there were two merchants;
they traveled together to conduct trade.
One sold real gold,
the second sold dūluó cotton.
Once, someone wished to buy real gold;
he burned it to test it.
The second merchant then secretly stole the gold that had been burned,
wrapped it in dūluó cotton;
but as the gold was hot, it burned up all the cotton.
When the truth was revealed, both parties lost out.
It is like those heretics
who steal the Buddha’s Dharma
and insert it into their own teachings,
falsely claiming it as their own—
but it is not the Buddha’s Dharma.
Thus,
they burn up and destroy their own texts,
which no longer circulate in the world;
just as when the gold was stolen,
the whole matter was exposed;
so too is it thus.
Long ago, there was a king
who owned a fine tree,
tall, broad, and extremely large,
which was to bear superior fruit,
fragrant and sweet.
At that time, a certain man
came before the king,
and the king said to him:
“This tree
will bear fine fruit.
Will you be able to eat it?”
He answered the king:
“This tree is so tall and large;
even if I wished to eat it, how could I possibly obtain it?”
He then cut down the tree
hoping thereby to get the fruit.
But he gained nothing at all,
only wearing himself out in vain.
Afterward he wanted to set the tree upright again,
but it had already withered and died,
without any life remaining.
Worldly people are also thus:
the Tathāgata, Dharma King, has a tree of precepts that can bear the finest fruit.
The mind gives rise to a wish
to taste the fruit,
so one should uphold the precepts
and cultivate all virtues.
But if one does not understand skilful means,
on the contrary destroys the precepts,
it is just like cutting down the tree,
and wanting to revive it again
is entirely impossible.
So it is also with those who break the precepts.
Long ago, there was a village
five yóuchún away from the royal city.
There was fine, beautiful water in the village.
The king ordered the villagers always to send the fine water to him each day.
The villagers were weary and worn out;
they all wished to move away from the village to a distant place.
At that time, the village chief addressed the people, saying:
“Do not leave!
I will petition the king for you,
to reduce the five yóuchún to three,
so that your travel may be nearer and you will not be tired.”
He went and petitioned the king;
the king changed it
to three yóuchún.
When the people heard this,
they were greatly delighted.
Someone said:
“But it has always been five yóuchún;
there is actually no difference.”
Even though they heard this,
because they believed the king’s word,
they would not abandon it.

Worldly people are likewise: cultivating the true Dharma to cross the five destinies toward the city of Nièpán, their minds grow tired and discouraged, and they wish to abandon it, halting midway in birth and death, unable to advance further. The Tathāgata, Dharma King, has great skillful means—within the One Vehicle Dharma he distinctly teaches three,
and those of the Small Vehicle are delighted when they hear this,
thinking it is easy to practice.
They cultivate good, increase virtue,
and seek to cross beyond birth and death;
later, when they hear others say,
“There are not three vehicles,
but truly one path,”
because they trust the Buddha’s words
they will not abandon it,
just like those villagers
who acted in the same way.
Once there was a man,
who was poor and destitute,
deeply in debt to others,
and had nothing to repay with;
so he escaped
to an empty, deserted place.
He came upon a chest
filled with precious treasures,
with a bright mirror
placed atop the treasure as a lid.
When the poor man saw this,
his heart was filled with joy;
he immediately opened it,
and, seeing a person in the mirror,
became startled and terrified.
Folding his hands he said,
“I thought this chest
was completely empty;
I never knew you were in here.
Please, do not be angry!”
Ordinary people are just the same:
impoverished by boundless afflictions,
bound and pursued by the creditors of Māra of birth and death,
they wish to escape birth and death
and enter the Buddha’s Dharma,
cultivating good practices
and performing all virtues.
It is like encountering a casket of treasures,
yet being deluded by the mirror of self-view,
mistakenly seeing a “self,”
immediately closing the chest again
and believing it to be real.
Thus they fall
and lose all merit—meditation, the components of the path, wholesome roots free of outflows,
the fruits of the three Vehicles—all are lost.
Just like that foolish man
who abandoned the chest of treasures,
so too is clinging to self-view.
Once there was a man
who entered the mountains to seek the Way
and became an immortal with the five supernatural powers.
With divine sight he could see through
and discern all hidden treasures within the earth.
The king heard of this,
and greatly rejoiced;
he said to his ministers:
“How can I ensure this man always remains in my country
and does not go elsewhere,
so that my treasury gains many riches?”
One foolish minister
immediately went
and gouged out both of the immortal’s eyes,
bringing them to the king saying,
“By gouging out his eyes,
he cannot leave again,
and must remain in this country.”
The king replied:
“The reason I wished to keep the immortal
was that he could see all hidden treasures in the earth;
you have now destroyed his eyes—
how can he be of any use?”
Worldly people are also like this:
seeing others cultivating ascetic practices—dwelling in mountains, forests, deserted graves, beneath trees—
practicing the Four Foundations of Mindfulness or contemplation of impurity,
they forcibly bring such people
into their households, lavishly supplying all they need,
thereby destroying their good practice
and obstructing the fruition of the path,
blinding the eyes of the Way;
having lost the benefit
they gain nothing at all,
just as that foolish minister
who senselessly destroyed another’s sight.
In former times, there was a man
who had two hundred and fifty head of cattle,
constantly driving them to water and pasture,
feeding them as the seasons required.
One time a tiger
devoured one of the cows.
At that time the owner thought to himself,
“I have already lost one cow;
now they are not complete.
What use are these cows to me?”
So he drove them all to a deep pit with high banks
and pushed them into the pit,
killing them all.
Foolish ordinary people are also like this:
after receiving and upholding the Tathāgata’s complete precepts,
if they break one and, without feeling shame or sincerely repenting and purifying themselves,
think to themselves,
“Since I have broken one precept,
I am no longer complete—
what is the use of observing the rest?”
They end up breaking them all,
not keeping a single one,
just as that foolish man
killed all his cattle
leaving not one alive.
Once there was a man
traveling who became thirsty and exhausted.
He saw that inside a wooden tube there was clear, pure water;
he went and drank from it.
After he had drunk his fill,
he immediately raised his hand
and said to the wooden tube:
“I have finished drinking,
so let the water no longer flow.”
Though he spoke these words,
the water continued to flow as before.
He then angrily said:
“I have already drunk my fill,
I told you not to come,
why have you come anyway?”
Someone saw this and said:
“You are very foolish
and lack wisdom!
Why do you not leave,
and when told not to come, continue to come?”
They immediately pulled him back,
dragging him away to another place.
People in the world are likewise:
due to the thirst of craving for birth and death,
they drink the brine of the five desires;
once wearied and sated by the five desires,
just like one who has drunk their fill,
they then say:
“You—forms, sounds, scents, and flavors—do not come again to make me see you.”
Yet these five desires continue without ceasing;
having seen them,
anger arises again:
“I told you to quickly end,
not to arise again.
Why do you come
and make me see you?”
At that time, a wise person spoke to him, saying:
“If you wish to be free,
you should restrain your six faculties,
close off your mind and intent,
and let false thoughts not arise;
then you will gain liberation.
Why act as if not seeing,
wishing that they do not arise?”
Just like that foolish man who drank the water—there is no difference.
In the past, there was a man
who went to another’s house
and found that the walls and structure had been well plastered,
the ground was level
and extremely clean and fine.
He then asked:
“What did you use to mix the plaster to make it so fine?”
The owner replied:
“I soaked rice husks
+ [麩-夫弋] in water to ferment them,
mixed them with clay to plaster the wall,
and thus achieved this effect.”
The foolish man immediately thought:
“If using only rice
+ [麩-夫弋] is not as good as mixing them with rice, and using that,
the wall will be white and clean,
and smooth and fine from the start.”
So he used unhusked rice mixed with clay
to plaster his wall,
hoping it would be flat and even;
instead it became uneven,
and the whole wall cracked.
He wasted the unhusked rice
and gained no benefit at all;
it would have been better to give it in charity,
to obtain virtue.
Ordinary people are also like this:
they hear the sages preach the Dharma
and cultivate all good deeds,
believing that when they abandon this body,
they will attain rebirth in heaven and liberation;
so they kill themselves,
hoping to be reborn in heaven and gain liberation,
but in vain, ruining themselves,
and gaining nothing at all—
just like that foolish man.
In the past, there was a man
with no hair on his head;
in winter he suffered greatly from the cold,
and in summer he was troubled by heat;
moreover, he was bitten and tormented by mosquitoes and gadflies,
suffering day and night,
and found it greatly painful.
There was a physician
skilled in many arts;
the bald man went to him,
and said to the doctor:
“I only wish that the master would cure me.”
The doctor himself was also bald;
he immediately removed his cap and showed him,
saying:
“I also suffer from this,
and consider it painful;
if I could cure it,
and recover from it,
I ought to first treat myself
and be rid of this affliction.”
People in the world are likewise:
they are tormented by birth, old age, sickness, and death,
and wish to find a place of immortality;
then hearing that there are shāmén and brāhmaṇa—excellent doctors in the world who skillfully cure all kinds of illness—
they go to them,
and say:
“I only wish you would rid me of this affliction of impermanent birth and death,
let me always dwell in happiness,
and be eternally unchanging.”
The brāhmaṇa and others then reply:
“I also suffer from this impermanence—birth, old age, sickness, and death;
I have sought many means to find the place of permanence, but in the end have never attained it.
If I could enable you to attain it,
then I should first attain it myself,
and then enable you to also attain it.”
Just like that bald sufferer,
merely laboring in vain,
and unable to recover.
In the past, there were two Pīshèluó demons
who jointly owned a chest, a staff, and a sandal;
the two demons quarreled
and each wanted the items;
they argued heatedly,
and after a whole day could not settle the matter.
At that time, a man
came and saw them,
asking:
“What is so marvelous about this chest, staff, and sandal
that you two quarrel
and are filled with anger?”
The two demons replied:
“This chest can produce all kinds of clothes, food, beds, bedding, and necessities for living— all come forth from within it.
Whoever holds this staff, all foes submit and none dare compete.
Whoever puts on this sandal, gains the ability to fly unhindered.”
Hearing this,
the man spoke to the demons:
“You two step back a little,
I will divide these fairly for you.”
When the demons heard this,
they immediately withdrew.
The man quickly seized the chest, took up the staff, put on the sandal, and flew away;
the two demons were astonished,
and gained nothing in the end.
The man said to the demons:
“The things you were fighting over, I have taken away;
now there is nothing left for you to quarrel over.”
The Pīshèluó demons symbolize the hordes of māra and heterodox paths.
Giving (dāna) is like the chest;
the resources and necessities for life among humans, devas, and the five realms all come forth from it.
Meditation (dhyāna) is like the staff;
it subdues the demonic enemies and thief of afflictions.
Observing precepts is like the sandal—
one will certainly ascend to the human and heavenly realms.
The various māras and heterodox paths quarreling over the chest symbolize those who, within their defiled states, strive forcibly for retribution,
but gain nothing.
Yet if one is able to practice good deeds as well as giving, keeping precepts, and meditation,
one will be freed from suffering
and attain the fruits of the Path.
