While traveling on business,
the merchant's group lost their camel suddenly on the road;
the camel had been carrying many treasures, fine silks, and various valuable goods.
Once the camel was dead,
they skinned it,
whereupon the head merchant left,
seating two disciples
and instructing them:
“Watch this camel hide well,
do not let it become wet and rotten.”
Later on, it rained;
the two, being foolish and obstinate,
covered the hide completely with fine silk,
so that all the silk was ruined and decayed.
The value of silk and camel hide is vastly different;
yet out of foolishness, they covered the hide with silk.
People in this world are the same:
abstaining from killing is like the white silk,
the camel’s hide represents wealth,
and the rain ruining it stands for negligent indulgence that destroys good deeds.
The precept of not killing is the supreme and most wondrous cause of the Dharma body of the Buddha;
yet if one cannot cultivate it,
but merely uses wealth to build various stupas and temples
and make offerings to the community of monks,
abandoning the root and taking the branches,
failing to seek the source,
one will drift among the five realms,
unable to extricate oneself,
so practitioners ought earnestly to uphold the precept of not killing.
It is like someone
who grinds a huge stone
with exertion and effort,
spending days and months,
only to make a little toy ox.
The labor is heavy,
but the expected result is trivial.
People in the world are likewise:
grinding the great stone is likened to study and learning,
diligently striving with hardship; making the little ox is likened to seeking name and reputation and fault-finding with one another.
As for scholars, they should study deeply, exhaustively, and gain broad knowledge;
they ought to put this into practice and seek far for the highest attainment;
but if they only pursue fame
and become arrogant and self-important,
they increase their faults.
It is like a person
who, due to hunger,
eats seven pancakes;
after eating six and a half,
he is full,
and then, resentful and regretful,
beats himself with his hand
and says:
"Now I am full
because of this half pancake.
The first six were wasted for nothing.
Had I known that only half would suffice,
I should have eaten it first."
People in the world are likewise:
since the beginning have always lacked true happiness,
yet in their delusion and inversion,
they arbitrarily imagine pleasure.
Like that foolish person
who, upon eating half a pancake, thought he was full,
people without understanding
take wealth and rank as happiness.
Wealth and rank involve great hardship to seek;
when one has acquired them,
guarding them brings more worry;
when one later loses them,
anxiety and grief arise again;
in all three phases, there is no real joy at all.
It is like clothing and food:
their ability to shield from cold and hunger is called happiness,
yet in toil and hardship people arbitrarily generate ideas of pleasure.
All Buddhas say:
"There is no peace in the three realms;
all is great suffering;
ordinary beings, in deluded confusion,
arbitrarily generate thoughts of happiness."
It is like a man
about to travel far,
who instructs his servant, saying:
"Guard the gate well
and also watch the donkey's rope."
After the master leaves,
there is music in a neighboring house,
and the servant wants to listen
but cannot be at ease himself.
So he ties the gate with the rope
and puts it on the donkey,
leads it to the place of entertainment,
and listens to the music.
After the servant leaves,
thieves take away all the goods of the house.
When the master returns,
he asks the servant:
"Where are the valuables?"
The servant replies:
"Master, you previously entrusted me with the gate, the donkey, and the rope;
beyond that, it is not within my knowledge."
The master says again:
"I left you to guard the gate precisely for the valuables;
now that the valuables are lost,
what is the use of the gate?"
The ignorant in birth and death, out of attachment to servants, are likewise:
the Tathāgata instructs
to always guard the gates of the senses,
not to cling to the six sensory objects,
to guard against the donkey of ignorance,
and to watch the rope of desire.
But monks do not follow the Buddha’s teaching,
greedily seeking gain,
and hypocritically appearing to be pure, sitting in quiet places,
while their minds are restless,
greedy for the five desires,
and confused by sights, sounds, smells, tastes,
ignorance clouds their minds,
and desire binds them with ropes;
their mindfulness, awareness, and the wealth of the path’s qualities are all lost.
It is as if the people of a village together stole a yak and ate it together.
The one who lost the ox traced it to the village,
called the villagers,
and questioned them,
saying:
"You are in this village."
The innocent replied:
"I really have no village."
He questioned again:
"There is a pond in your village;
did you all eat the ox by the pond?"
The reply: "No pond."
Questioned again:
"Is there a tree by the pond?"
The reply: "No tree."
Questioned again:
"When you stole the ox, was it east of your village?"
The reply: "No east."
Questioned again:
"Was it not midday when you stole the ox?"
The reply: "No midday."
He asked again:
"Even if there is no village or no tree,
how can there be no east or no time in the world?
I know your words are false and not to be trusted.
Did you eat the ox or not?"
The reply:
"Indeed, I ate it."
So too with breakers of precepts:
they hide their faults,
unwilling to disclose them,
and when they die, fall into hell.
The heavenly gods and good spirits look upon them with their divine eye;
they cannot conceal their sins,
just as those who ate the ox
cannot lie or refuse to admit it.
Long ago, in a foreign country, on the festival day, all women would wear udbala flowers for adornment.
There was a poor man,
whose wife said:
"If you can obtain an udbala flower
and bring it to me,
I will remain your wife;
if you cannot,
I will leave you."
The man, having formerly mastered the sound of the Mandarin duck,
entered the royal pond
and imitated the duck's call,
stealing some udbala flowers.
The pond guard asked:
"Who is in the pond?"
The poor man unwittingly replied:
"I am a Mandarin duck."
The guard seized him
and brought him before the king.
On the way, he again imitated the duck's cry,
making the Mandarin duck sound.
The pond guard said:
"You did not do so before;
now, what use is it?"
Worldly fools are also like this:
all their lives they harm and destroy,
committing all sorts of evil deeds,
not cultivating their minds,
nor training themselves toward virtue;
only at the time of death
do they say: "Now I wish to do good."
The guardians of hell take them to Yánluó Wáng;
though they may wish to cultivate goodness,
it is already too late,
like that foolish man
hoping to reach the king
by making the sound of a Mandarin duck.
It is like a jackal under a tree;
the wind breaks a branch,
which falls on its back.
It immediately closes its eyes
not wishing to look at the tree,
and flees away
into the open;
even until dusk,
it does not return.
From afar, it sees the wind moving the great tree’s branches swaying up and down,
and then says, calling out to it,
and goes to the tree.
Foolish and ignorant disciples are just like this:
having left home and
coming close to a teacher,
at the slightest rebuke, take flight;
yet later, encountering evil companions
who constantly trouble them,
they return
to the place they had left—thus repeatedly leaving and returning, displaying their folly.
It is as in ancient times when two children entered a river to play;
beneath the water, they found a handful of hair.
One child said:
"This is a sage’s beard."
The other said:
"This is a bear’s hair."
At that time, by the riverbank there was a xiānrén,
and these two young boys quarreled ceaselessly.
They went to the place of the xiānrén
to resolve their doubts.
That xiānrén immediately took rice and sesame seeds,
chewed them in his mouth,
spat them out onto his palm,
and said to the boys:
"What is in my palm looks like peacock droppings."
But this xiānrén did not answer their question;
everyone knew this.
Worldly fools are just the same:
when explaining the Dharma, they engage in frivolous talk about various dharmas,
and do not answer in accord with the true principle.
Just as that xiānrén did not answer the question,
they are ridiculed by everyone.
Idle, vain talk is likewise.
For example, someone
suddenly suffers from a curved spine
and asks a physician for treatment.
The physician applies ghee as an ointment,
attaches boards above and below,
and forcefully presses with great pain;
unaware, both eyes pop out at once.
Worldly fools are likewise:
in order to cultivate merit,
they engage in trade and business,
committing many non-Dharmic acts.
Though matters may be accomplished,
the gain does not make up for the harm,
and in the future they will fall into hell, which is likened to the popping out of both eyes.
For example, five people jointly buy a maid.
Among them, one tells the maid:
"Wash clothes for me."
Next, another person also tells her to wash clothes.
The maid responds to the second:
"First, I am to wash for the previous one."
The latter gets angry and says:
"I, together with the former, jointly bought you.
Why are you serving only him?"
Thereupon, he whips her ten times.
Thus, all five each beat her ten times.
The five skandhas are also thus:
Afflictions and causes together result in this body,
and these five skandhas constantly, by birth, aging, sickness, and death, inflict immeasurable suffering and beating upon sentient beings.
For example, there is a performer
who plays music before the king,
and the king promises a thousand coins.
Later, the performer asks the king for it,
and the king does not give it,
but says:
"Your earlier performance
was empty music for my ears,
so also my giving you money
would just be empty delight for your ears."
The results of karma in this world are also thus:
though one enjoys a little pleasure among humans or in heaven,
it is not real,
being impermanent, subject to destruction, not lasting long,
like that empty music.
For example, a teacher has two disciples.
The teacher has pain in his foot,
and sends the two disciples, each to attend to one foot and massage it as needed.
These two disciples always hate and envy each other.
When one disciple is away,
the other grabs the foot he is supposed to massage and smashes it with a stone;
after the first returns,
in anger at what happened,
he also grabs the foot the other was attending and immediately smashes it.
Buddhist students are also just like this:
those who study Mahāyāna disparage the Hīnayāna,
Hīnayāna students in turn disparage the Mahāyāna;
thus, the great canon of the sages perishes in both ways.
For example, there is a snake,
whose tail says to its head:
"I should be in front."
The head says to the tail:
"I am always in front,
why suddenly do you want this?"
When the head is in front,
the tail wraps around a tree,
unable to move forward;
letting the tail go first,
it immediately falls into a pit of fire
and is burned to death.
Teachers and disciples are likewise:
saying the teacher is old and experienced,
always to be in front.
We, the younger, should be the leaders instead.
Thus, the young who do not understand the precepts
commit many offenses;
as a result, they drag each other into hell.
In ancient times, there was a king
who had a trusted retainer.
On the battlefield, he risked his life to save the king, ensuring his safety.
The king was greatly pleased
and granted whatever he wished.
He asked:
"What do you seek?
You may have whatever you desire."
The minister answered:
"When wáng shaves his beard, I wish to be the one to shave it."
The wáng said:
"If this is your wish,
I grant you what you desire."
Such a foolish person is mocked by the world;
when half a kingdom, or the counsel of a great minister could be obtained,
instead he asks for a menial task.
Fools are like this:
all the buddhas, through countless kalpas, endured difficult ascetic practice to attain buddhahood.
If one encounters the Buddha or comes across the Dharma and obtains a human body—which is hard to attain
like a blind turtle encountering the hole in a floating log—
these two things, so hard to meet,
now already met,
yet their aspiration is inferior;
keeping just a few precepts, they think it is enough,
and do not seek the supreme and wondrous Dharma of nirvāṇa;
with no mind for diligent progress,
but acting with wrong conduct,
they think it is sufficient.
Once there were two people
traveling together on a road.
They saw a man with a sesame cart, who, on a dangerous path,
could not move forward.
The cart-pusher said to the two:
"Help me push the cart out of this dangerous spot."
The two replied:
"What will you give us?"
The cart-pusher said:
"I have nothing to give you."
Still, these two helped push the cart
to flat ground.
They said to the cart-pusher:
"Give us something now."
He replied: "I have nothing."
Then again they said:
"Give us 'nothing.' "
Of the two, one smiled and said:
"He won't give us anything; why be troubled?"
The other replied:
"If you give me 'nothing,'
surely there ought to be some 'nothing.' "
The one said:
" 'Nothing,' these two words together
are but a false name."
Worldly ordinary people, clinging to 'nothing,'
are born in the state of non-possession.
The second person says
that 'nothing' means without appearance, without desire, without action.
In former times there was a great and wealthy elder.
Those attending him wanted to please him,
and were all entirely respectful.
Whenever the elder spat,
his attendants immediately stomped it away with their feet.
One among them, a fool, was always too slow to stomp it away,
and then thought:
"When he spits on the ground,
others always stomp it away first.
When I want to stomp, I am always too late.
So, next time he is about to spit,
I must stomp first."
Just then, as the elder was about to cough and spit,
the fool immediately lifted his foot and stomped on the elder's mouth,
breaking his lips and teeth.
The elder said to the fool:
"Why did you stomp my lips and mouth?"
The fool replied:
"If you spit out and it lands on the ground,
the fawning attendants always get to stomp it first.
Even though I wish to stomp, I'm always too late.
Therefore, when you are about to spit, I lift my foot and stomp in advance,
hoping to win your favor."
All things require the right time.
If the time has not yet come,
forceful effort
will only bring suffering.
Therefore,
people should know what is timely and what is not.
who fell gravely ill
and knew that death was certain.
He instructed his two sons:
"After my death, divide the wealth evenly."
The two sons followed his instructions,
and after his death divided the inheritance into two parts.
The elder brother said
the younger brother's share was unfair.
Then a foolish old man said:
"Let me show you how to divide the goods
so that it will be equal.
Take all current possessions and break them into two.
How to break them?
That is, cut the clothes in half,
crack the plates and bottles into halves,
break up all the pots and kettles into halves,
and split the coins in two.
In this way, all possessions are completely broken, then divided into two."
This way of dividing things brings ridicule from others.
For example, various wàidào
are partial in their cultivation and explanations,
and there are four types of debate methods:
the method of giving a decisive answer,
such as saying “All humans must die,”
this is the method of decisive answer in debate.
“Whoever dies must have been born,”
this is an answer requiring distinction;
“Who ceases craving will have no further birth,”
“Where there is craving, there is birth,”
this is called the method of distinction answer in debate.
If someone asks, “Are humans the most excellent?”
one should answer by asking in return:
“Are you asking about the three evil paths?
Or are you asking about the various heavens?
If you ask about the three evil paths,
then humans are indeed the most excellent;
but if you ask about the heavens,
humans are certainly inferior.”
Such meanings as these are called the method of answering by returning the question.
If asked about the Fourteen Difficult Questions,
such as whether the world and sentient beings are finite or infinite, or have a beginning or end, or have no end or beginning,
such questions are called the method of setting aside the answer in debate.
The various wàidào are foolish and ignorant,
yet think of themselves as wise.
They break apart the four types of debate
and create only one type of distinction debate,
like a foolish person dividing up money and possessions,
breaking a coin into two pieces.
For example, two people went to a potter’s place,
watching as he pressed the wheel and made clay jars,
and watched without ever getting enough.
One person left,
went to a great assembly,
there obtained the finest foods
and gained precious treasures;
one person watched the jars
and said,
“Let me keep watching.”
In this way, lingering on and on until sunset,
he kept watching the jars
and missed out on clothing and food.
The foolish are likewise;
attending only to their household affairs
and not realizing the impermanence.
Today busy with this matter,
tomorrow creating that business,
when the Tathāgata Dà Lóng appears,
thunderous voice spreads throughout the world,
the Dharma rain pours without hindrance,
yet because of circumstances, they do not hear it.
Not knowing that death suddenly arrives,
they miss this assembly of all the Buddhas,
and fail to obtain the precious Dharma jewels,
always dwelling in poverty in evil destinies.
Turning away and abandoning right Dharma,
they gaze only at circumstance-bound clay jars,
always and forever without end,
thus losing the benefit of the Dharma,
and never find a time for liberation.”
Once, there was a foolish man
who went to a great pond,
and saw a reflection of real gold at the bottom of the water,
he believed there was gold there,
and entered the water
stirring up mud to search for it.
Exhausted with effort and finding nothing,
he came up and sat again.
After a while, the water cleared
and the golden color appeared again,
so he went back in
stirred up the mud and searched again,
yet again he could not obtain it.
It happened that, just then, his father came searching for his son
found him and asked,
“What are you doing,
to be so tired and worn out?”
The son told his father,
“There is real gold at the bottom of the water,
so I went in
wanting to stir the mud and take it,
but though I have exhausted myself, I cannot get it.”
The father looked at the reflection of the gold at the bottom of the water
and knew the gold was actually on a tree,
for this reason: the reflection shows up at the bottom of the water.
The father said,
“It must be that a bird carried the gold and placed it on the tree.”
So, following his father’s words, the son climbed the tree and obtained it.
Ordinary foolish people,
lacking wisdom, are just so;
within the aggregates that are not-self,
they mistakenly generate the conception of self;
just as that man saw the gold’s reflection,
toilsomely seeking,
laboring in vain and gaining nothing.”
The assembly of Bōluómén all say:
“Mahā-Brahmā King is the father of the world,
the creator of all things.”
The creator has disciples, and those disciples say,
“I too can create all things,”
but truly, they are foolish and ignorant
and claim to have wisdom.
They speak to Brahmā:
“I want to create all things.”
Brahmā King replies,
“Do not attempt this;
you cannot create them.”
Not heeding Brahmā’s words,
the disciple proceeds to create things.
When Brahmā saw what the disciple had made,
he said:
“You’ve made the head too large,
the neck extremely small,
the hands too big,
the arms extremely short,
the feet extremely small,
the heel extremely large,
it looks like a Pi Shě Chá ghost.”
From this, one should know: each is shaped by their own karma; it is not Brahmā who creates.
The Buddhas, in teaching the Dharma, do not cling to either extreme;
nor to annihilation
nor to eternity,
but speak the Dharma as with the Noble Eightfold Path.
The various wàidào,
once seeing the extreme of annihilation and the extreme of permanence,
then give rise to attachment,
deceiving the world
making forms and images as their teaching,
but in truth, what they teach is not Dharma.
Once, there was a man
gravely ill,
and a skilled physician diagnosed him, saying:
“You must always eat one kind of pheasant meat,
then you will be cured.”
The sick man went to the market and got a pheasant,
ate it all up
and did not eat any more.
Later, when the physician saw him, he asked:
“Is your illness cured yet?”
The sick man replied:
“The physician previously instructed me to always eat pheasant meat,
so after eating this one pheasant, I did not dare eat more.”
The doctor said again:
“If the previous pheasant is gone, why not eat another?
How can you expect your illness to be cured by eating only one pheasant?”
All wàidào are just the same:
hearing the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, the supreme good physicians, say,
“You must understand mind and consciousness,”
the wàidào and the like cling to the view of permanence,
and thus say that past, future, and present are only one consciousness,
unchanging and without ceasing,
just as eating only one pheasant,
therefore, they cannot cure the disease of ignorance and affliction.
The great wisdom Buddhas teach the wàidào to remove their view of permanence:
All dharmas arise and perish from moment to moment;
how could there be a single consciousness that is eternal and unchanging?
Just as a worldly doctor’s prescription to eat another pheasant cures the illness,
so too the Buddha,
teaching all sentient beings,
enables them to realize
that all dharmas decay and are thus not permanent, and by continuing, are not destroyed,
and thus eradicate the illness of the view of permanence.
Long ago, in Qián Tuó Wèi Guó, there were some performers,
in a time of famine, seeking food in other lands,
passing by Póluólá New Mountain,
which, in that mountain, was long inhabited by fierce demons and flesh-eating rākṣasas.
Those performers happened to stay in the mountain overnight,
and as the mountain wind was cold,
they made a fire to sleep.
There was one performer who, feeling cold,
put on a costume that had once belonged to a rākṣasa,
and sat by the fire.
Then, one of the group who woke from sleep, suddenly saw a rākṣasa by the fire,
and without looking carefully,
fled at once,
alarming the others,
so the whole company fled in panic.
The one wearing the rākṣasa garment also set off and
ran after them with all his might,
but his fleeing companions, seeing him behind,
thought he intended them harm,
and were even more terrified,
crossing mountains and rivers,
plunging into valleys and ravines,
injuring their bodies,
collapsing exhausted
until morning came,
at last realizing it was not a demon.
All ordinary people are just the same:
Living in the famine of afflictions and having few wholesome dharmas,
yet seeking after ever-lasting happiness, self, and supreme purification,
thus within the five aggregates arbitrarily postulate the self.
Because of the view of self, they are swept away in saṃsāra,
driven by afflictions, never attaining freedom,
falling into the gulfs of the three evil paths,
and “morning comes” is a metaphor for the end of the night of saṃsāra;
with the illumination of wisdom, they then know the five aggregates do not contain any real self.
In the past, there was an old house.
People said that this room was always inhabited by evil ghosts,
and all were terrified,
daring not to sleep there.
At that time, there was a man
who claimed to be very courageous,
and he said:
“I wish to enter this room
to spend a night sleeping inside.”
He then went in and stayed the night.
Later, another man
claimed that his bravery surpassed the previous person’s,
and upon hearing from others that evil ghosts always dwelled in that room,
he also wished to enter,
pushing open the door, about to step forward.
The one who had entered first thought he was a ghost,
so he pushed the door closed and refused to let him enter.
The one coming behind also thought there was a ghost,
and the two argued and fought.
When dawn came, and they saw each other, they realized they were not ghosts.
All people in the world are also like this—
circumstances come together briefly with no true master.
Each tries to discern, “Who am I?”
Yet sentient beings arbitrarily dispute right and wrong,
and forcibly give rise to argument and contention,
just like those two men, with no difference.
In the past, there was a woman
who was wanton and unrestrained in lust.
Her desires were so intense
that she grew to hate her husband.
She constantly plotted
and schemed to harm him,
using all sorts of tricks,
but could not find the opportunity.
As it happened, her husband was commissioned to a neighboring country.
The woman secretly made a plan
and manufactured poison pills,
intending to use them to harm her husband.
She deceitfully said to her husband:
“You are now going far away,
and may suffer hunger or want.
I have prepared five hundred joy pills
to be provisions
to send with you.
If you go abroad to another region,
you may eat them only when truly hungry or weary.”
The husband believed her words.
After reaching the foreign land,
he had not yet eaten them,
and at night stayed in a forest.
Fearing wild beasts,
he climbed a tree to escape.
He forgot and left the joy pills at the foot of the tree.
That night, five hundred thieves happened to pass by,
having stolen five hundred horses and treasures from that country’s king,
and stopped below the tree.
Because they had fled hurriedly,
they were all hungry and thirsty.
At the bottom of the tree, they found the joy pills.
The thieves took them,
each ate a pill,
and because the poison was strong,
all five hundred thieves died at once.
At dawn,
the man on the tree saw the group of thieves dead below.
Pretending, he slashed and shot the corpses with sword and arrows,
then collected their saddles, horses, and treasures,
and drove them to that country.
At that time, the country’s king led many people
to trace the tracks in pursuit.
Meeting him midway,
the king asked:
“Who are you?
Where did you get these horses?”
The man replied:
“I am a man of a certain country.
On the road, I encountered this group of thieves.
We battled with swords and arrows,
and now the five hundred thieves all lie dead together under a tree.
Therefore I obtained these horses and treasures
and have come to pledge them to your kingdom.
If you do not believe me,
you may send someone to check—the mark of their wounds and the scene where they died.”
The king immediately sent a trusted person to check,
and it was just as he said.
The king was overjoyed
and praised it as something unprecedented.
After returning to the country,
he lavishly bestowed titles and rewards,
and granted him large treasures,
enfeoffing him with a village.
All the former ministers of the king became jealous and reported to the king:
“He is a foreigner,
not to be easily trusted.
How can you treat him with such favor so suddenly,
granting him honors and rewards
that surpass the established ministers?”
When the foreigner heard, he said:
“Who among you has courage to compete with me?
Let us meet on the open plain to test our skills.”
The old ministers were astonished, and none dared oppose him.
Later, in the great wilderness of that country, there was an evil shīzǐ
that blocked the way and killed people,
cutting off the king’s road.
The ministers discussed among themselves:
“That foreigner claims no one can match his courage.
If he can now kill this shīzǐ to rid the country of harm,
truly that would be extraordinary.”
After deciding, they informed the king. Upon hearing,
the king immediately gave him sword and staff and sent him out.
The foreigner received the order,
hardened his resolve,
and went to where the shīzǐ was.
The shīzǐ saw him
and rushed forward, roaring fiercely.
Terrified,
the foreigner quickly climbed a tree.
The shīzǐ opened its mouth,
raising its head towards the tree.
In his fright,
the man lost hold of his sword,
which fell into the shīzǐ’s mouth.
The shīzǐ died at once.
The foreigner rejoiced greatly,
and reported to the king.
The king doubled his favor,
and all the people of the country naturally respected him,
all praising him.
The woman’s joy pills are a parable for impure charity.
The king dispatching a messenger is a parable for the good spiritual friend.
Traveling to another country is a parable for the devas.
Killing the group of thieves represents attaining srotaāpanna and decisively severing the five desires and all afflictions.
Meeting the king is a parable for encountering a wise sage.
The former ministers’ jealousy is a parable for how outsiders slander those with wisdom who can sever afflictions and the five desires,
saying such things are impossible.
The foreigner’s fierce claim that none of the old ministers can rival him is a parable for outsiders not daring to oppose in debate.
Killing the shīzǐ is a parable for defeating Māra.
Having cut off afflictions and subdued evil Māra,
one obtains the reward and title of the fruition of detachment.
Being always fearful is a parable for being able to use the weak to overcome the strong.
Though at first there was no pure mind,
when charity encounters a good spiritual friend,
it gains great merit.
If even impure charity can bring this,
how much more so pure and joyful charity?
Therefore, one should diligently practice giving in the field of merit.

In the past, there was a son of a great elder,
who entered the sea with merchants to search for treasure.
This elder’s son was skilled in reciting the method of navigating a ship at sea:
if one enters places in the sea with whirlpools, eddies, and crashing waves,
one should hold like this,
set straight like this,
steady like this,
and he told everyone:
“I fully know the method of crossing the sea.”
When the people heard this, they deeply believed his words.
Once they reached the middle of the sea,
not much time had passed before the boatman fell ill
and suddenly died.
At this time, the elder's son immediately took his place.
When they arrived at the whirlpool and swift current,
he called out,
“You must hold it like this, steer it like this.”
The boat spun round and round,
unable to advance toward the treasure,
and all the merchants on board drowned and died.
Ordinary people are also like this:
with little practice of the meditation methods such as mindfulness of breathing and contemplation of impurity,
though reciting the words without understanding their meaning,
they truly know nothing of the various methods,
yet claim to be skillful in understanding,
and recklessly transmit meditation methods,
causing those before them to become confused and lose their minds, and to distort the marks of the Dharma.
For years and years they gain nothing,
just as the foolish man caused others to drown in the sea.
In the past, there was a husband and wife
with three bánh (steamed cakes).
The husband and wife divided them,
each ate one,
and one was left.
They made an agreement together,
“If anyone speaks, they will forfeit the cake.”
Having made the agreement,
for the sake of that one cake neither dared to speak.
After a short while, a thief
entered the house to steal,
and took their valuables,
all of their possessions were carried off by the thief;
the husband and wife, because of their previous agreement, watched silently without speaking.
The thief saw them silent,
and right in front of the husband violated the wife.
The husband saw it with his own eyes, yet still did not speak.
Then the wife called out to the thief
and said to her husband,
“How can you be such a fool? Just for a cake, you see the thief and don’t call for help?”
Her husband clapped his hands and laughed, saying,
“Ha! Woman,
I have surely won the cake,
and will not give it to you.”
Everyone who hears this laughs at it.
Ordinary people are also like this:
for the sake of petty reputation or profit, they falsely appear silent,
and are invaded by the many evil thieves of false and troubling desires,
lose their good Dharma,
fall into the three evil destinies,
and are entirely unafraid,
having no wish to seek the way out of the world.
Instead, regarding the five desires,
they become attached and indulge in play,
even when suffering greatly
they do not consider it a misfortune.
They are just the same as those foolish people.
Once there was a man,
who became angry with someone else,
and was full of worry and unhappiness.
Someone asked him,
“Why are you now so troubled and weary?”
He replied,
“Someone slandered me,
and I am powerless to repay him.
I don’t know how or where I could get revenge,
so that is why I am worried.”
The other said,
“Only the mantra pí tuó luó can harm him,
but there is one problem:
before it can harm the other, it will first harm yourself.”
The man, hearing this, was overjoyed,
“Please just teach me,
even though it will harm myself, I still hope to hurt him.”
Worldly people are also like this:
because of anger, they wish to seek the pí tuó luó mantra
in order to trouble another,
but before they can harm others,
they themselves are first troubled and harmed by anger,
falling into hell, the animal, and hungry ghost realms,
no different from that foolish man.
Once there was a man
who came from Běi Tiānzhú to Nán Tiānzhú.
After staying a long time, he married a woman and they became husband and wife.
The wife prepared food and drink for him,
which the husband would swallow hurriedly,
not minding the heat.
His wife found this strange,
and said to her husband,
“There are no thieves or robbers here,
so what is the urgency
that you are in such a rush
and do not eat calmly and slowly?”
The husband replied to his wife,
“There is a very secret matter
that cannot be told to you.”
When the wife heard this,
she thought he had some extraordinary method,
and earnestly asked him about it.
After a long time he finally answered:
“From my grandfather onward
it has always been our family’s way to eat quickly.
I now follow this,
so I eat fast.”
Worldly foolish people are also like this:
not understanding the true principle
nor knowing good from evil,
doing all sorts of wrong actions
without any sense of shame,
and saying,
‘From my grandfather onward, we have always done this,’
practicing it until death
never abandoning it,
just as that foolish man clung to eating quickly as good practice.
Once there was an elder,
who sent someone with money to another orchard
to buy mangoes
because he wanted to eat them,
and instructed him, saying:
“You must buy those that are good and sweet.”
He then took the money and went to buy the fruits.
The owner of the orchard said:
“All the mangoes on these trees are delicious,
not a single bad one.
Taste one fruit
and you will know.”
The buyer said:
“Now I must taste them all
before choosing.
If I taste only one,
how can I be sure?”
He then took the fruits
and tasted each one,
and brought them home.
The elder, seeing this,
found them distasteful and would not eat them,
and so discarded them all.
Worldly people are also like this:
hearing that keeping precepts and giving brings great wealth and joy,
the body always peaceful and free of suffering,
they will not believe it,
and say:
“If giving brings blessings,
I will only believe it once I have received them myself.”
Yet they see plainly in this world that nobility and baseness, wealth and poverty, are all the result of past deeds and their retribution,
but do not know how to reason from one example to understand cause and effect,
and instead remain unbelieving,
waiting to experience it themselves.
But once they die,
they lose all possessions and wealth,
just like tasting the fruits
and then discarding them all.
Once there was a man
who married two wives.
If he got close to one, the other would be angry.
Unable to decide,
he lay directly between the two wives, flat on his back.
As it happened, great rain fell from the sky,
and the roof leaked,
both water and mud fell
into his eyes.
Because of the prior agreement,
he did not dare to get up and move aside,
and thus both his eyes were blinded.
Ordinary worldly people are also like this:
associating with bad friends,
learning and practicing wrong ways,
accumulating bad karma,
falling into the three evil destinies,
long remaining in birth and death,
losing the eye of wisdom,
just as that foolish man lost both eyes because of his two wives.
Once there was a man
who went to his wife's house,
and saw her pounding rice.
He went to her
and secretly stuffed his mouth with rice.
The wife came and saw her husband
and wanted to speak with him,
but with his mouth full of rice
he would not reply,
and out of shame before his wife
would not spit it out,
and so did not speak.
The wife was puzzled by his silence,
and touched his mouth with her hand,
thinking his mouth was swollen,
and said to her father,
“My husband just came,
and suddenly his mouth became swollen,
and he cannot speak at all.”
Her father then called a doctor to treat him.
The doctor said,
“This illness is severe;
with a knife to cut it open,
he can perhaps be healed.”
Even if one uses a knife to cut open his mouth,
rice will come out from within,
and the matter will be clearly revealed.
People in the world are likewise;
when committing evil deeds
and violating pure precepts,
they conceal their faults
and are unwilling to confess them,
falling into hell, animal, or hungry ghost realms.
Like that foolish man,
out of a little shame, he would not spit out the rice;
only after cutting his mouth open with a knife
did his fault become apparent.
In former times, there was a man
who rode a black horse
into battle to fight against bandits.
Because of his fear, he could not fight,
so he smeared his face with blood
and feigned the appearance of death,
lying among corpses.
The horse he rode was taken by another.
When the troops withdrew,
he wished to return home,
so he cut off the tail of someone else’s white horse
and, upon reaching home,
someone asked him:
"Where is the horse
you were riding
—why do you not ride it?"
He replied:
"My horse is dead,
so I brought its tail back."
A bystander said:
"Your horse was black;
why, then, is the tail white?"
He was silent, without reply,
and became the laughingstock of others.
People in the world are also like this;
they claim themselves to be virtuous
and practice compassion,
abstaining from alcohol and meat,
yet they kill living beings
and inflict torture,
falsely claiming goodness
while committing every evil,
like that foolish man
who feigned his horse was dead.
In former times, a king
established a teaching:
That all brāhmaṇas and others within his country must be purified by washing,
and those not washed were driven to perform all kinds of harsh labor as punishment.
There was a brāhmaṇa who only pretended to hold water for bathing,
falsely claiming he was washed.
If anyone poured water over him,
he would immediately pour it away.
Then he would say:
"I am not washing;
the king must do it himself."
To escape the king’s labor, by the king’s wish,
he falsely claimed to be purified,
when in truth he was not.
Common monks are likewise:
having their heads shaven and their robes dyed,
but inwardly breaking the precepts,
feigning observance of the rules
in hopes of gaining offerings and to avoid the king’s service,
outwardly resembling a śrāmaṇa,
but inwardly full of deceit,
like holding an empty bottle
that only has the outward appearance.
In former times there was a man
who first filled a jar with grain.
A camel put its head into the jar to eat the grain
and could not get out.
Unable to withdraw, it became distressed.
An old man came and said to it:
"Do not be worried!
I will teach you how to get out.
If you follow my words,
you will surely get out quickly.
You should cut off your head
and then you yourself will get out."
Taking his advice,
he used a knife and cut off the head,
killing the camel and breaking the jar.
Such a fool is laughed at by the world.
Ordinary foolish people are also like this:
setting their hearts on bodhi,
aspiring for the three vehicles,
and ought to maintain prohibitions
and guard against evil,
but for the sake of the five desires they violate the pure precepts,
and once the prohibitions are broken, they abandon the three vehicles,
letting loose their minds to perform all evil,
and cast aside both the vehicles and the pure precepts,
like that fool who lost both camel and jar.
In former days there was a farmer
who was traveling through cities and towns,
and saw the guówáng’s daughter,
whose appearance was most exceptional
and rare in the world.
Day and night he thought of her,
unable to stop his feelings,
longing for union
with no way to accomplish it.
His complexion became ashen yellow,
falling into serious illness.
Seeing this, his family and friends asked him: "Why are you like this?"
He replied to his relatives:
"Yesterday I saw the guówáng’s daughter,
whose appearance was most beautiful.
Longing for union with her but unable to obtain it, I have become ill for this reason.
If I cannot have her,
I will surely die, there is no doubt."
His family said:
"We will make a good plan for you,
so that you may get her.
Do not worry."
Later, upon seeing him,
they said:
"We have arranged for this for you,
only the guówáng’s daughter is unwilling."
When the farmer heard this,
he joyfully smiled,
thinking he would surely obtain her.
Foolish people in the world are likewise:
they do not discern the proper seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
so they sow seeds in the ground in winter
hoping to gain fruit,
but only lose their labor
and gain nothing,
with sprout, stalk, branch, and leaf all entirely lost.
Foolish people in the world practice a little merit
and think it sufficient,
saying that bodhi can thus be attained,
as that farmer hoped for the guówáng’s daughter.
In former days, people on the frontier did not know what a donkey was;
they heard others say that donkey’s milk was very delicious,
but none of them understood.
At that time, people got hold of a male donkey,
and wanted to obtain its milk,
arguing as they seized it:
some grabbed its head,
some its ears,
some its tail,
some its legs,
and some held a container,
each wishing to be first
to drink from it.
Among them, someone grabbed the donkey’s penis
thinking it was the udder,
and tried to milk it
hoping to get its milk.
All became tired and annoyed,
but gained nothing,
laboring in vain
and getting nothing at all,
and became the laughingstock of all the world.
Heterodox commoners are likewise:
they hear talk of the Way,
but seek it where they should not,
giving rise to false thoughts,
developing all kinds of wrong views,
going naked and starving themselves,
casting themselves onto cliffs or into fire;
through these wrong views they fall into evil destinies,
like those foolish people vainly seeking milk.
In former times there was a man,
who, during the night, said to his son:
"Tomorrow, I will take you to that village
to get something."
Having heard this,
at daybreak,
without asking his father,
the son went there alone.
When he arrived,
his body was utterly exhausted,
yet he gained nothing,
and, without food,
hungry and thirsty nearly unto death,
he returned,
and came to see his father.
When the father saw his son,
he sternly rebuked him, saying:
"You are truly foolish,
lacking in wisdom.
Why did you not wait for me?
You went forth in vain,
needlessly suffering,
and have become the laughingstock of all the world."
Ordinary people are also just like this:
Suppose they leave home
and have their beards and hair shaved off,
wear the three Dharma robes,
but do not seek an enlightened teacher
for guidance in receiving the Dharma,
they lose all the meditative concentration
and merits of the paths and fruits of a shāmén; all are completely lost.
Like that foolish man
who makes a vain journey back and forth,
exhausting himself to no purpose,
resembling a shāmén in appearance
but truly gaining nothing.
In the past, there was a king
who wished to enter the Garden of No Sorrow
to enjoy amusements and pleasures.
He ordered a minister, saying:
"You, carry a stool
and bring it to the garden
so I may use it to sit and rest."
The servant at that time was too ashamed to carry it
and spoke to the king, saying:
"I cannot carry it.
I would rather bear it on my back."
So the king put thirty-six stools on his back
and drove him to carry them into the garden.
Thus this fool is laughed at by the world,
and ordinary people are likewise:
If they see a woman's strand of hair on the ground
they claim to keep precepts
and will not pick it up;
but later, deluded by afflictions,
they handle without shame thirty-six things—hair, fur, nails, teeth, excrement, urine, all impure substances—
holding all thirty-six things at once
without any feeling of shame,
and do not give them up even unto death,
like that fool bearing the stools.
In the past there was a man
who suffered from a lower body illness.
His doctor said:
"You must have medicine administered by enema to be cured."
So, all the appliances for the enema were gathered
in order to use them for the treatment.
While waiting for the doctor to arrive,
he took the medicine himself and swallowed it.
His belly swelled as if he would die,
and he could not endure it.
When the doctor arrived,
he was surprised and asked
what had happened:
"Why is it like this?"

He answered the doctor, "A little while ago, I took the enema medicine orally, so I am about to die." The doctor, hearing this, rebuked him deeply, saying, "You are a great fool and do not understand expedient means." He then administered another medicine, which caused him to vomit and purge, and only then did he recover. Such a fool is laughed at by the world,
and ordinary people are just the same:
they wish to cultivate meditation,
contemplating various methods;
when they ought to practice impurity contemplation,
they instead count the breath;
when they ought to count the breath,
they contemplate the six elements;
reversing the order up and down,
without any foundation,
vainly losing life and body,
troubled and entrapped by this.
Not consulting good teachers,
their meditation practice is utterly confused,
like that fool who swallowed the impure medicine.
In the past, there was a father and son
traveling with companions;
the son entered a forest
and was bitten by a bear,
whose claws wounded his body.
In distress, he escaped the forest
and returned to his companions.
The father saw the son's body injured and damaged,
and asked him in astonishment,
"Why have you now suffered these wounds?"
The son replied to his father:
"There is a kind of creature
with shaggy hair
that came and hurt me."
The father, taking up bow and arrows,
went to the forest,
and saw an immortal
with long, dense hair,
and was about to shoot him.
A bystander said:
"Why are you shooting at him?
This person has done no harm;
you should punish the guilty one instead."
Ignorant people in the world are also like this:
because of criticism from those who wear Dharma robes but have no moral conduct,
they slander and harm good and virtuous people,
just like that father
whose son was wounded by a bear but who wrongly attacked the immortal.
In former times, there was a rustic
who came to the fields,
saw fine wheat sprouts
growing lush and abundant,
and asked the owner of the wheat:
"How can these sprouts be made so flourishing?"
The owner replied:
"Level the land,
and add manure and water as well,
thus it grows as you see."
The man then acted according to this instruction,
mixing water and manure
to prepare his field,
sowing seeds in the earth.
Fearing that his own feet would trample the ground and make it too hard for the wheat to grow,
"I will sit on a bed
and have others carry me,
so I can scatter the seed from above;
only then will it be good."
So he had four men
each lift one leg of the bed,
and carried him into the field to scatter the seed.
The ground became even more compacted,
causing people to laugh at him.
Lest his own two feet
add to the four men's eight, increasing the harm.
Ordinary people are likewise:
having cultivated the field of precepts
so that good sprouts are about to grow,
they ought to seek a teacher
to receive instruction and admonishments,
to let the sprouts of Dharma grow;
instead, they turn to violations
and do much evil,
causing the sprouts of precepts not to grow,
like that man
who feared his own two feet
and instead added eight more.
Once there was a monkey
who was struck by an adult,
but, unable to do anything in return,
turned his resentment on a child.
Ignorant people are also just so:
the person they were angry at
is no longer present,
passed into the past,
yet toward something connected and arising later they believe it is the former person;
thus they give rise to deluded anger
and their poison and hatred only deepen,
just as that foolish monkey
was beaten by an adult and instead got angry at a child.
Long ago, Āxiūluó Wáng saw the sun and moon shining brilliantly
and tried to block them with his hand;
foolish ordinary people, like dogs who are blameless but are attacked without reason.
So, too, with ordinary people:
Greed, anger, and delusion
continually afflict themselves,
lying on thorns and brambles
tormented by the five fires,
just like the eclipse of the moon
and those who wrongfully beat the dog.
Once there was a woman
who suffered greatly from eye pain.
A woman friend asked her:
"Does your eye hurt?"
She replied:
"Yes, my eye hurts."
The other woman said:
"If one has eyes, pain is inevitable.
Though I have not yet suffered pain
I want to gouge out my eyes
lest they later hurt."
A bystander said:
"If you have eyes, they may or may not hurt;
if you don't have eyes, you will be in pain for life."
Ignorant people are just the same:
hearing that wealth and nobility are the roots of decline and affliction,
they fear giving nothing,
and dread future retribution,
and when wealth overflows
they bear even more suffering and affliction.
Someone might say:
"If you give, there may be sorrow or happiness;
if you do not give, there is great hardship in poverty."
Just like that woman,
unable to endure present pain,
wanting to remove her eyes
only to end in lasting misery.
In the past, there was a father and son
who traveled together on an errand.
On the road, robbers suddenly appeared
intending to rob them.
The son's ears had true golden earrings.
The father, seeing the robbers about to rush in,
fearing the loss of the earrings,
pulled at his son's ears with his own hands,
but the earlobe would not immediately tear off,
so for the sake of the earrings, he cut off his son's head.
In a short while, the robbers fled and left.
When he tried to put the son's head back on his shoulders
it could not be restored.
Such fools are laughed at by the world.
Ordinary people are just the same;
for the sake of fame and profit, they construct speculative arguments,
saying there is existence in both lives or that there is nonexistence in both lives;
there is an intermediate state, there is no intermediate state;
there are mental factors, there are no mental factors;
with all sorts of deluded imaginings, they do not attain the reality of dharma.
When others refute their arguments with correct principles,
they then say:
“My argument does not say any such thing at all.”
Such foolish people, for the sake of a little fame or profit, knowingly speak falsely,
thus losing the fruits of the Śāmén path.
When their bodies decay and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil destinies,
like those foolish people
who, for a little profit, behead their own child.
Long ago, there was a band of thieves
who together set out to steal and rob.
They obtained much wealth and goods
and then divided it together,
making the portions equal.
Only a deerskin of Lùyě Qīnpóluó, which was not pure in color,
was considered a lesser share
and given to the one least skilled.
The inferior one, receiving it, grew angry
and cried out over his great loss.
Arriving at the city, he went to sell it;
the noble elders gave him a high price.
He alone got twice what his companions obtained,
and only then was he exceedingly joyful and delighted beyond measure.
It is just as ordinary people
do not know whether giving brings reward or not,
yet with only a little giving, they are born in heaven and receive boundless happiness.
Only then do they regret,
regretting that they did not give more broadly.
Just like the Qīnpóluó,
who later got a great price and then became delighted;
so it is with giving:
with little effort, one gains much,
and only then does one rejoice,
regretting not having done more.
Long ago, there was a monkey
holding a handful of beans.
By mistake, one bean fell to the ground.
He then discarded the beans in his hand
to go searching for that one.
Before finding the one bean,
the beans he had discarded were eaten up by chickens and ducks.
Ordinary people who leave home are just the same;
at first, for breaking one precept
they cannot repent,
and because they do not repent
their negligence grows,
and they abandon everything,
like that monkey
who, for the sake of one bean lost,
cast away all he had.
Long ago, there was a man
traveling along a road.
On the way, he obtained a golden mangustāna (mongoose),
and his heart rejoiced;
he put it in his bosom,
walked on,
and when he reached water and wished to cross,
he took off his clothes and placed them on the ground.
Suddenly, the golden mangustāna turned into a poisonous snake.
The man deeply mused:
“I'd rather be bitten and killed by the poisonous snake
but must carry it with me.”
His heart, being sincerely moved,
it turned back again into gold.
A foolish man watching from the side saw his poisonous snake turn into real treasure,
and thought it was always thus.
He too took a poisonous snake,
placed it in his bosom,
and was promptly bitten by the snake,
losing his life.
Foolish people in the world are just the same;
seeing the good gain benefit,
but without a true heart within,
merely for the sake of profit and gain do they attach themselves to the Dharma,
but after death they fall into an evil destination,
just like one grasping a poisonous snake
and being bitten to death.
Long ago, there was a poor man
traveling on the road.
By chance, he obtained a bag of gold coins.
His heart leaped in great joy,
and immediately he began to count them.
Before he could finish counting,
the owner of the gold suddenly arrived
and took back all the money.
At that moment, the man regretted not having left quickly
and his grief was immeasurable.
Those who encounter the Buddha Dharma are just the same;
though able to encounter the field of blessings of the Three Jewels,
they do not diligently cultivate skillful deeds,
and when death comes unexpectedly,
they fall into the three evil destinies,
just like that foolish man
who had his money taken away by its owner.
As the verse says:
“Today busy with this affair,
tomorrow involved in that one;
clinging to pleasure, not seeing suffering,
not realizing the thief of death arrives.
Hurriedly busy with myriad tasks—
there is no one among mortals who is not thus.
Like the one who counts his money,
so it is with men and their affairs.”
Long ago there was a poor man with but little wealth.
Seeing those greatly rich,
he wished to be their equal.
Unable to match them,
though he had little wealth, he wished to throw it in the water.
A bystander spoke,
“This may be little, but it could still preserve your life a few days more.
Why do you discard it
and toss it in the water?”
Foolish people in the world are just the same;
though they have left home
and receive only a little support,
their hearts aspire
and constantly feel unsatisfied.
Unable to match those of higher virtue
and receive their support,
they see others of old virtue,
long possessed of much learning and many offerings,
and desire to be like them,
but being unable to match them,
they are filled with anxiety and suffering,
and so wish to abandon the path—
just like that foolish man
who wanted to be equal to the rich
and so threw away his own wealth.
Long ago, there was a nurse
holding a child as she traveled a road.
Fatigued from the journey,
she fell asleep unawares.
At that moment, a man
offered a sweet ball to the child.
The child, delighted by its flavor,
did not look after himself or his belongings.
That man then took off his restraints, jewelry, and clothes
and carried them all away.
So too with the bhikṣu:
delighting in worldly affairs,
in noisy and clamorous places, greedy for a little gain,
the thief of afflictions steals away all his merit and the jeweled necklaces of morality,
just like that child
who, greedy for a small taste,
had all he possessed stolen away.
Long ago, there was an old woman
lying beneath a tree.
A bear came wanting to seize her.
The old woman circled the tree fleeing.
The bear chased close behind.
She grasped the trunk with her arms
while the bear tried to seize her.
The old woman, acting quickly,
clasped the tree and pinned the bear’s arms with it,
so the bear could not move.
Another stranger arrived then.
The old woman said,
“You and I will hold it and kill it, and divide its meat.”
The man believed what the old woman said,
and so helped hold it.
After it was captured,
the old woman let go of the bear and ran away,
and the man was left to be mauled by the bear.
Such fools are mocked by the world.
Ordinary people are just the same:
they produce various strange arguments
that are not skillful or good;
their writing is verbose
and full of errors,
and in the end is never completed.
Then they abandon and leave it unfinished,
while others take up
and try to explain it,
but not understanding its meaning,
are only further confused by it—
just like that foolish man
who helped catch the bear for another but ended up harmed himself.
Long ago, there was a man
who had illicit relations with another’s wife.
Before their affair was finished,
the husband came from outside
and discovered them,
standing outside the door
waiting for the man to come out
so he could kill him.
The wife said to the man:
“My husband knows,
and there is no way out
except by escaping through the máoní.
(The máoní,
in Qí language, means ‘water drain hole.’)” She wished the man to escape through the water drain.
That person misunderstood
and said it was a Máoní pearl;
he sought everywhere
but did not know where it was,
and then said:
“If I do not see the Máoní pearl,
I will never leave.”
In a short while, he was killed because of it.
Ordinary people are the same:
someone says:
“In saṃsāra
there is impermanence,
suffering, emptiness,
and no-self.
Avoid the two extremes of annihilation and eternity,
abide in the Middle Way.
Passing through here,
one may attain liberation.”
The ordinary person misunderstands,
and seeks for whether the world is finite or infinite, or whether beings have self or not;
in the end, they cannot contemplate the principle of the Middle Way,
and when death suddenly comes,
they are killed by impermanence,
and fall into the three evil destinies,
just like that foolish person
who sought the Máoní
and was harmed by others.
In the past, there were a male and a female pigeon
who shared a nest;
in autumn, when the fruits ripened, they gathered the fruit and filled their nest.
Later, the fruit dried up and decreased,
and only half a nest remained.
The male, angry at the female, said:
“Collecting the fruit was hard work;
you ate it alone,
that’s why only half is left.”
The female pigeon replied:
“I did not eat it alone;
the fruit naturally lessened.”
The male pigeon did not believe her,
spoke angrily and said:
“If you did not eat it alone,
why would it have decreased?”
Then he pecked the female pigeon to death.
Not many days passed,
a great rain fell from heaven;
the fruit became moist again
and returned to its original state.
The male pigeon saw this
and felt deep regret:
“She truly did not eat it;
I wrongly killed her.”
He cried out in grief, calling for the female pigeon,
“Where have you gone?”
Ordinary people are the same;
deluded thoughts fill their hearts,
they vainly pursue sensual pleasures
without contemplating impermanence,
commit the gravest offenses
and only regret afterwards,
but what use is it then?
In the end, they only wail in sorrow,
just like that foolish pigeon.
In the past, there was an artisan
who worked for the king,
but could not endure the hardship.
Falsely claiming to be blind,
he thus escaped his suffering.
Another craftsman heard this
and wanted to destroy his own eyes
in order to avoid forced labor.
Someone said:
“Why do you harm yourself?
You only endure suffering in vain.”
Thus, the foolish person is laughed at by the people of the world.
Ordinary people are also like this:
for a little fame or profit, they deliberately lie,
break pure precepts,
and when their bodies die and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil destinies,
just like that fool
who, for petty gain,
destroyed his own eyes.
Once, there were two people traveling together in a vast wilderness.
One wore a woolen garment;
halfway, they were robbed by bandits;
one fled
and ran into the grass.
The one who lost the garment had earlier wrapped a coin in the collar,
and said to the robbers:
“This garment is worth only a single coin;
I ask that you let me ransom it for one coin.”
The robber said:
“Where is the coin now?”
Thereupon, from the collar he untied it and showed them,
and said to the robbers:
“This is real gold.
If you do not believe me,
there is a fine goldsmith hiding in the grass here;
you may ask him.”
The robbers, seeing this,
took his garment as well.
Thus, that fool lost both garment and coin,
losing his own benefit
and causing the other to lose as well.
Ordinary people are likewise:
cultivating the Path,
performing all kinds of virtuous deeds,
are plundered by the bandits of afflictions,
lose their wholesome Dharma,
and forfeit their merits.
Not only do they lose their own benefit,
they also cause others to lose their progress on the Path.
When their bodies perish and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil destinies,
as that fool
who made both lose.
Once, there was a young boy
playing on land,
who caught a large turtle.
Wanting to kill it
but not knowing how,
he asked someone:
“How can I kill it?”
Someone replied:
“Just throw it into water,
and it will instantly die.”
At that time, the boy believed his words and threw it in the water;
the turtle, having entered the water,
immediately swam away.
Ordinary people are the same:
wanting to guard their six senses
and cultivate merits,
but not knowing how.
They ask others:
“Through what cause can I attain liberation?”
Wrong views, outside paths, Mára Póxún, and evil companions say to them:
“Just indulge your six senses, pursue the five desires to the utmost;
if you follow my words,
you will surely attain liberation.”
Thus, these fools do not consider carefully,
but follow their advice,
and when their bodies perish and their lives end,
they fall into the three evil destinies,
just as the boy threw the turtle into the water.
This treatise, which I have composed,
blends in jest and laughter
and contains many informal or less-than-literal statements;
one should examine the meaning to see whether it is appropriate.
It is like a bitter, poisonous medicine
mixed with rock honey—
the medicine eliminates illness,
and so does this treatise.
Humor within true Dharma
is like potent medicine;
the Buddha’s true Dharma is tranquil and serene,
its brightness illumines the world.
As with emetic medicine,
combined with butter to moisten the body,
so I now use this meaning
to reveal serenity.
Like the Agada medicine
wrapped in a leaf,
when the medicine is applied to the poison,
the leaf is thrown away.
Jesting is like the wrapping leaf,
the true meaning is within.
The wise take the true meaning,
and cast away the joking.
Venerable Sēngjiā Sīnà composed the 'Garland of Foolish Flowers.'
